# Shepherd of Hermas Chapter 89 — The PNEUMA Bible (Dynamic)

**Translator:** PNEUMA | **Source:** Codex Athous, Shepherd of Hermas 89 | **Source Image:** source-texts/greek-EC/SHE_089_page_001.jpg

---

## Similitude 9 — The Twelve Mountains

**1** "And the twelve mountains — what do they represent?" I asked. "They represent twelve peoples spread across the whole world," he said. "The Son of God was proclaimed to all of them through the apostles." **2** "But why are they all so different? Some were rough and rocky, some bare with nothing growing, some covered in thorns and thistles, some desert wasteland, some covered in the richest green grass, some hilly, some flat, some gleaming white — why such variety?" **3** "Listen carefully," he said. "These twelve mountains represent twelve peoples. **4** The first — the black mountain — represents those who have renounced the faith, blasphemed the Lord, and betrayed fellow believers. There is no repentance available for them. That's why they are black: their category is death. **5** The second — the bare mountain with nothing growing — represents hypocrites who made a profession of faith but bear no fruit of authentic living. Just as that mountain has no plant and no fruit, these people profess Christianity but produce no genuine results. They still have a chance to repent — if they turn back quickly, the death hovering over them won't catch them. **6** The third — covered in thorns and thistles — represents those who believed but then became wealthy and got entangled with the culture around them. The thorns and thistles of that entanglement strangled their faith so that nothing bears fruit anymore. These can still repent if they return quickly. If they wait too long, they'll die alongside those who never believed. **7** The fourth — with many plants, green on top but withered at the bottom — represents the half-committed: neither truly alive nor dead. They're like people who can never make up their mind — suspended between life and death."

---

*PNEUMA renders the mountain typology as a diagnostic portrait of different Christian communities, emphasizing the pastoral urgency of repentance.*
